subsections.subsection_title: Important Peripheral Signs to Know for OSCEs

blocks.text: If you're in an OSCE and need to perform it efficiently, use this sequence:

“I would complete my examination by examining the respiratory system for pulmonary edema, the abdomen for hepatomegaly and ascites, and performing a full peripheral vascular examination. I would also review the patient's observations, medication history, ECG, chest X-ray and relevant blood tests.”
For exams, make sure you can recognize these five patterns quickly:
Slow-rising pulse + heaving apex + ejection systolic murmur + carotid radiation

Absolutely. For clinical exams, knowing how to perform the cardiovascular examination is only half the skill. You also need to be able to report your findings fluently, identify the likely diagnosis, justify it with findings, and answer follow-up questions from the examiner.

subsections.subsection_title: How to Report a COMPLETELY NORMAL Cardiovascular Examination

blocks.text: At the end of your examination, don't simply say:

“This is a [age]-year-old [male/female] who is comfortable at rest and not in obvious respiratory distress. There is no peripheral cyanosis, pallor or clubbing. The peripheral extremities are warm with normal capillary refill. The pulse is regular at 72 beats per minute, of normal volume and character, with no radio-radial or radio-femoral delay. Blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg.

The JVP is not elevated. The carotid pulses are normal with no carotid bruits. The apex beat is palpable in the 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line and is not displaced. There is no parasternal heave or palpable thrill.
S1 and S2 are normal, with no added heart sounds or murmurs. There is no peripheral edema.

items: Overall, there are no significant abnormal cardiovascular findings.”

subsections.subsection_title: Short Version for a Time-Pressured OSCE

blocks.text: “This patient is clinically stable. They have a regular pulse of 72 bpm with normal volume and character and a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg. The JVP is not elevated. The apex is not displaced, with no parasternal heave or thrill. S1 and S2 are normal with no added sounds or murmurs. There is no peripheral edema. Overall, there are no significant abnormal cardiovascular findings.”
Don't jump immediately to the diagnosis. Report the physical findings first, then give your interpretation.

“The pulse is slow rising and of reduced volume. The apex beat is heaving. There is an ejection systolic murmur maximal in the aortic area with radiation to the carotids. These findings are suggestive of aortic stenosis.”

There is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur best heard along the left sternal edge with the patient sitting forward in expiration. These findings are consistent with aortic regurgitation.”

On auscultation, S1 is loud with an opening snap followed by a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumbling murmur best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position. These findings are suggestive of mitral stenosis, complicated by atrial fibrillation.”

subsections.subsection_title: Common OSCE "Why Did You Do That?" Questions

content_groups.group_title: “Why did you check the patient's hands?”

blocks.text: To assess peripheral perfusion and look for signs such as clubbing, cyanosis, splinter hemorrhages and other peripheral manifestations of cardiovascular disease.

content_groups.group_title: “Why did you check both radial pulses?”

blocks.text: To assess symmetry and identify radio-radial delay or unequal pulses.

content_groups.group_title: “Why did you check the femoral pulse?”

blocks.text: To assess peripheral perfusion and look for radio-femoral delay, which may suggest coarctation of the aorta.
To assess carotid pulse character and detect carotid bruits.

content_groups.group_title: “Why only one carotid at a time?”

blocks.text: To avoid compromising cerebral blood flow.
To assess right atrial pressure and systemic venous congestion.

content_groups.group_title: “Why did you listen in the axilla?”

blocks.text: To assess radiation of murmurs, particularly mitral regurgitation.

content_groups.group_title: “Why did you ask the patient to sit forward?”

blocks.text: To accentuate the early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation.

content_groups.group_title: “Why did you put the patient in the left lateral position?”

blocks.text: To accentuate low-frequency sounds at the apex, particularly mitral stenosis.
